This paper analyzes the underlying drivers of these forecast misses by leveraging two novel global datasets on tax policy yields and tax administration capacity. It finds that tax revenue-to-GDP forecast errors are primarily driven by over-optimism in forecasted yields of tax policy measures and tax buoyancy assumptions, as well as macroeconomic forecast errors, particularly for growth and trade openness. Stronger tax administration capacity and well-implemented and high-quality revenue related structural reforms are associated with lower forecast errors. Additional empirical analysis shows that over-optimism in forecasted tax policy yields declines significantly when revenue measures are well-designed, part of large-measure revenue packages, and accompanied by high-quality revenue-related structural reforms. Improving forecast realism requires better-grounded yield estimations and tax buoyancy assumptions, explicit consideration of implementation capacity, and a focus on well-designed revenue-related structural reforms.
focus_rationale: The paper uses global cross-country datasets on tax policy yields and administration capacity across IMF-supported programs, with no particular economy or region as its focus.

title: Recurring Natural Disasters and Macroeconomic Scarring
abstract: Recurring climate-related natural disasters pose significant macroeconomic and fiscal risks for highly exposed countries. We extend the Debt, Investment, Growth, and Natural Disasters (DIGNAD) model to incorporate Annual Average Loss (AAL) metrics, capturing the cumulative macro-fiscal effects of repeated natural disaster shocks. The augmented DIGNAD framework introduces recurring annual capital losses and negative productivity shocks, yielding more realistic growth and public debt trajectories under persistent disaster risk. We quantify the GDP losses from recurrent natural disasters and examine the trade-offs between higher adaptation investment (leading to higher recovered growth) and public debt accumulation. Using cross-country simulations for 33 disaster-prone economies and case studies (the Philippines, Mauritania, and Barbados), we find substantial heterogeneity in disaster impacts and adaptation effectiveness. Comparing risk-adjusted baseline projections with scenarios of scaled-up resilient vs. standard infrastructure investment, we find that investing in resilient public capital can significantly mitigate output losses in the long-term, albeit at the cost of higher public debt.
focus_rationale: The paper runs cross-country simulations for 33 disaster-prone economies, which are mainly developing and emerging, and uses case studies of the Philippines, Mauritania and Barbados. Its focus is on the macro-fiscal effects of disasters in these countries.

title: The Global Fiscal Actions (GFA) Dataset
abstract: We introduce the Global Fiscal Actions (GFA) Dataset, the first quarterly global narrative database of discretionary fiscal policy actions, covering 142 countries since 1990. GFA combines Economist Intelligence Unit country reports with large language models to systematically identify and classify tax and spending measures, together with their motivations, timing, implementation status, and supporting evidence. We validate the dataset against economists' assessments, existing narrative datasets, fiscal aggregates, and repeated AI extractions, demonstrating high accuracy and reproducibility. We illustrate its value through applications to fiscal cyclicality and country-specific fiscal multipliers, providing new evidence on the conduct and effectiveness of fiscal policy worldwide.
focus_rationale: The dataset covers 142 countries worldwide, spanning advanced and emerging economies, so it has no single market focus.

title: Effectiveness of Monetary Policy Transmission in Morocco amid Reforms to the Monetary Policy Framework
abstract: This paper assesses the effectiveness of Morocco’s monetary policy transmission since 2018 in light of reforms aimed at modernizing the policy framework. Over the past decade, Morocco has introduced greater exchange rate flexibility, strengthened the legal and operational focus on price stability, and enhanced central bank communication—measures intended to anchor inflation expectations and improve transmission. Drawing on several years of post-reform data, we use a two-step empirical strategy: (i) identifying exogenous monetary policy shocks through a Taylor-rule-based approach leveraging Bank Al-Maghrib’s forecasts, and (ii) estimating their dynamic effects via local projections, a flexible approach well suited to settings with structural change and limited data. Our findings indicate that transmission to output and inflation has strengthened post-reform: a 1 percentage point policy rate hike reduces output by about 0.3 percent and inflation by 0.1 percent, compared to 0.1 and 0.05 percent pre-reform, respectively. However, responses remain delayed and muted relative to benchmark estimates for other emerging markets. Analysis of transmission channels shows the interest rate channel is most active, the credit channel is partially effective, and the exchange rate channel is stronger post-reform, while the asset price and expectations channels remain weak. These findings provide important insights for Morocco’s ongoing transition to an inflation targeting regime.
focus_rationale: The paper studies monetary policy transmission in Morocco, an emerging market, using post-reform data and benchmarking against other emerging markets.

title: Price Gouging and the Monopoly Option
abstract: We investigate a dynamic oligopoly model with two phases: a normal phase where an essential input is available, and a disruption phase where firms must rely on inventories. Disruptions create an overcutting pricing incentive arising from the option to forgo sales and monopolize the market once rivals stock out. This monopoly option causes the price to jump to a supracompetitive level at the advent of the disruption and to remain above the competitive price path throughout. Price caps raise welfare, but reduce inventory investment. Government reserves reduce prices and raise buffer stocks, as do reserve mandates when financially feasible.
focus_rationale: The paper is a theoretical dynamic oligopoly model with no specific economy studied, so it is Transversal.

title: Bank liquidity regulation and the growth of private credit
abstract: We study the role of bank liquidity regulation in the growth of private credit. Following the introduction of the liquidity coverage ratio (LCR), private credit increases significantly more in U.S. counties with a larger footprint of banks subject to the LCR or of LCR banks with greater initial liquidity shortfalls.
focus_rationale: The paper studies U.S. counties and the U.S. bank liquidity coverage ratio, so it is about an advanced economy.

title: The Why and How of Foreign Aid
abstract: Foreign aid has become a melting pot of motivations and policies, where differently-motivated actors often converge on recommended policies while the similarly-motivated diverge.Breaking down the "why" and the "how" can illuminate real tensions and reveal false ones.The "why" asks which problems to tackle and who benefits: the recipient, the donor through economic, political, or soft-power returns, or everyone through global public goods.The "how" asks which strategy most cost-effectively addresses a chosen problem.Evidence is central to the "how": use it where it exists, produce it where it does not.In particular, approaches which improve state capacity to use and generate evidence can satisfy multiple objectives: strengthen recipient countries, benefit donors, and provide a global public good of knowledge.Ultimately, the "how" is not a linear process, but rather an iterative one of learning, adopting, adapting, repeating, and then sharing so others can learn as well.
focus_rationale: The paper is a general discussion of foreign aid motivations and strategies, with no particular economies studied. It is global and cross-country in scope.

title: Correcting for Heterogeneity in the Use of Subjective Scales
abstract: Analyses of survey data may be confounded if people use response scales differently.We formalize and generalize the theory behind using "calibration questions," such as vignettes, to correct for scale-use heterogeneity.Finding, in our (N 10,000) and existing data, that the mapping between respondents' scales is approximately linear, we develop a simple estimator for scale-use-corrected regressions.We validate it using subjective-scale ratings of height and weight and illustrate it with life satisfaction regressions, where correction leaves the main qualitative findings intact but can substantially change coefficient ratios, for example tripling the estimated cost of unemployment relative to income.
focus_rationale: The paper is a methodological contribution on correcting survey scale-use heterogeneity, validated on height and weight ratings and illustrated with life satisfaction regressions, with no particular economy as its focus.

title: Too Little too Late? Nationwide Carbon Trading in China
abstract: China launched a nationwide, rate-based carbon market in 2021.Covering the world's top CO2 emitter, compliance depends on the intensity of carbon emissions rather than an absolute cap.We draw on the theoretical literature of rate-based systems to provide the first empirical evidence on an early adopter.Using plant-level data from satellite imagery and machine learning methods, we find that high-efficiency power plants increased electricity generation and CO2 emissions by approximately 5% relative to low-efficiency plants.Because its carbon market regulates nearly all coal plants in China, we focus on the differential responses by plant efficiency, finding no evidence of a differential reduction in emission intensity (though these estimates are imprecise).Relative to coal plants in Indonesia and the Philippines, which had no carbon market, China's high-efficiency plants also increased emissions, while the estimate for its low-efficiency plants is small and insignificant.This pattern of responses suggests that emissions increases of highefficiency plants exceeded substitution away from low-efficiency plants.Underscoring the production stimulus to more efficient Chinese plants, air quality worsened downwind of highefficiency plants relative to low-efficiency plants, compromising air quality in relatively clean areas of China.If China's goal is to reduce its carbon emissions, then benchmarks will need to be tightened within the existing system or an alternative system that does not simultaneously incentivize electricity production will need to be adopted.
focus_rationale: The paper studies China's nationwide rate-based carbon market and compares Chinese coal plants with plants in Indonesia and the Philippines, so the economy studied is China, an emerging market.

title: Will Medical Care Strangle or Save the Federal Budget?
abstract: Forecasts of the federal budget depend greatly on trends in medical spending.Since 1970, medical spending has nearly tripled as a share of gross domestic product (GDP).However, spending growth has barely exceeded GDP growth since 2010.This difference in growth rates makes forecasting spending difficult.I present scenarios for future spending derived from considering the sources of spending increase, ranging from rapid increases in new, expensive treatments to a reduction in spending due to cost-reducing technology.Even modest increases in spending relative to GDP are likely to overwhelm the federal government's ability to pay for medical care using current tax instruments.
focus_rationale: The paper studies US federal budget and medical spending trends, so it is about an advanced economy, the United States.

title: The Role of Organization in Firm-Sponsored Training
abstract: Some firms are more likely than others to invest in workers' skills.We document this phenomenon and discuss its implications in light of models of firm-sponsored skills training.The data show that better managed firms, even in the same industries and labor markets, are more likely to train, while training clusters around either managerial or frontline worker development.We argue that organizational differences provide incentives for firms to train beyond traditional explanations that focus on labor market frictions.We illustrate how organizational heterogeneity can generate training investments through a knowledge hierarchy framework where top managers with different skills build bespoke organizations tailored to their unique needs.This in turn makes general skill firm-specific, allowing firms to capture returns on training investment.
focus_rationale: The abstract does not name specific economies; it draws on cross-firm data and a theoretical knowledge hierarchy model, with no particular country focus.

title: Venture Capital and Customer Capital
abstract: Venture capital specializes in the financing of customer capital intensive firms-firms with higher sales and marketing expense to revenue ratios, a higher wage bill for sales and marketing employees, and a higher tendency to apply for trademarks-and they do so more than other financial intermediaries.Venture capitalists target high customer capital industries with low knowledge capital but avoid high knowledge capital industries that lack customer capital.Firms tilt investment toward customer capital leading up to the initial venture capital investment, after which their scale accelerates rapidly.Venture capitalists focus on financing customer capital because such investments require tolerance for substantial risks of failure in pursuit of extreme upside potential, as characterized by power law returns.This return profile fits customer capital investments more closely than investments in knowledge capital.Venture capitalists that sprinkle small investments across a large number of firms, colloquially referred to as the "spray and pray" strategy, target customer capital industries for investment, whereas venture capitalists that commit larger amounts to a small number of firms target knowledge capital industries.The venture capital focus on customer capital reflects a shift away from its traditional focus on knowledge capital intensive firms over the past 30 years.
focus_rationale: The paper studies US firms financed by venture capital and other intermediaries, so it is mainly about an advanced economy. It is a US-centred study of venture capital and intangible customer capital.

title: Firms' Investment and the Real Transmission of the Global Financial Cycle
abstract: We study how global financial conditions transmit to firms' investment.We document that increases in risk premia are followed by large investment contractions, particularly among firms with higher default risk.We develop a quantitative heterogeneous-firm open-economy model where firms finance investment with defaultable debt priced by risk-averse global investors.We identify a strong risk channel linking changes in the global price of risk to financing costs through firms' quantity of risk-the sensitivity of debt repayment to global shocks.This introduces a risk dimension to stabilization policy: smoothing cash flows reduces firms' quantity of risk and dampens international financial transmission.
focus_rationale: The paper studies the transmission of global financial conditions to firm investment using a cross-country, open-economy framework without a specific focus on one economy group, so it is best classed as Transversal.

title: The Effects of a Shorter Workweek on Employment, Output, and Productivity
abstract: Do shorter workweeks generate work-sharing and productivity gains, as intended by policymakers?We study France's pay-preserving reduction in the workweek from 39 to 35 hours, bundled with employer payroll tax cuts.We first exploit the staggered implementation by firm size to identify the impact of the reform package.We then use differential exposure to the hours cut and tax cut to separate their effects.We combine matched employer-employee, balance-sheet, and survey data to study worker, firm, and local labor market effects.The reform package left employment unchanged.This zero masks large offsetting effects: absent the tax cuts, the shorter workweek would have reduced employment by 3.8%.The effects are skill-biased, raising employment among managers and professionals while reducing it among other employees.Finally, shorter hours raised total factor productivity by 2%, limiting the output decline to 1% despite a 6% fall in total hours.Surveys point to work intensification and organizational changes as potential drivers of productivity gains.
focus_rationale: The paper studies France's 2000s-era workweek reduction from 39 to 35 hours bundled with payroll tax cuts, a single advanced economy in the euro area.

title: Transportation as a Barrier to Education Access: Evidence from Chicago Public Schools
abstract: School choice can weaken the link between residential neighborhood and educational opportunity only if students can reach the schools available to them.We study school choice in Chicago, where high schoolers can choose among schools throughout the city but generally rely on public transit, making the structure of the transit network a key determinant of opportunity.Using student-level rankings and public transit travel times, we document two systematic patterns: Black students are less likely to rank top-rated schools first and face longer public transit times to such schools.We estimate a discrete choice model to separate the value placed on schools from the costs of reaching them.We find that high schools vary substantially in how they are valued and that there is a high degree of agreement across racial groups in their relative ranking.However, transit times vary significantly across neighborhoods, generating racial differences in demand for top-rated schools.Counterfactually, giving Black students the travel times of white students increases demand for top-rated schools by 23 percentage points.Finally, we identify underserved neighborhoods where public transit access constrains demand and quantify how targeted bus service would increase demand for high-quality schools.Our counterfactuals quantify how transportation expands school access.
focus_rationale: The paper studies school choice and public transit access within a single US city, Chicago, so it is a US-only study rather than a DM or EM focus. Its market focus is best described as Transversal because it is not an advanced-economy macro or financial study, but the study is US-based.

title: The Impact of the Great Recession on Mortality: A Dynamic Factor Analysis
abstract: We use a dynamic factor time series model to estimate the national mortality impact of the Great Recession.In aggregate, the Great Recession reduced the average annual, age-adjusted mortality rate by about 2 percent, with effects persisting for at least a decade.In a calibrated model of the welfare effects of the estimated impacts of the Great Recession on consumption and mortality, we find that the welfare gain from the estimated mortality decline is quantitatively significant relative to the welfare loss from the estimated consumption decline.The estimated mortality decline is also quantitatively close to prior mortality estimates using cross-sectional variation in the severity of the Great Recession, implying limited general equilibrium effects of the Great Recession on mortality.More broadly, our findings suggest that prior evidence from local labor markets that recessions are good for health can be extrapolated to the likely mortality consequences of nationwide recessions.
focus_rationale: The paper studies the national US mortality impact of the Great Recession, so it is about an advanced economy.

title: Upgrading Financial Markets
abstract: Expanding access to financial services may not be enough to develop markets in low-income settings: providers also need to be held accountable to consumers.We test this in a field experiment across 195 rural Sierra Leonean communities, upgrading Village Savings and Loan Associations (VSLAs) into mobile money and bank agents, cross-randomized with a monthly consumer feedback mechanism.Upgrading expands access, but feedback drives large operational improvements (+20.5 pp, 85%), particularly in privacy and consumer protection, raising usage and revenues.Upgraded VSLAs also show higher savings digitization and higher incomes, evidence that disciplining agent actions benefits not only consumers but also the principal that finances and stands behind its agent.Interpreted through a framework of delegated intermediation, we show accountability, not infrastructure alone, aligns provider incentives with consumer welfare and is central to designing scalable financial intermediaries.
focus_rationale: The paper is a field experiment in rural Sierra Leone, a low-income economy, studying mobile money and bank agents for village savings groups. It is development finance with little direct link to market pricing or macro policy.

title: Green Subsidies with Demand Distortions
abstract: Credit constraints and other demand distortions are pervasive in lower-income contexts.A model of clean technology adoption shows that demand distortions can increase the welfare gains from green subsidies.This arises through two channels: shifting the marginal adopter toward higher private and social benefits, and increasing demand elasticity.We test this by cross-randomizing purchase price subsidies, usage subsidies, and access to an interest-free loan for a US$84 induction stove among 2,134 charcoal users in Kenya.Usage subsidies of 75% have a precise zero effect on adoption and usage.Purchase price subsidies, however, generate large welfare gains.Credit constraints raise the subsidy's efficacy by 35%-73%, up to US$10-US$12 in observable welfare gain per subsidy dollar.This demand distortion also lowers the subsidy cost of abatement by 41%, to US$12 per tCO 2 e.This operates through the two channels identified in the theory: credit constraints raise the marginal adopter's positive externality by 19% and fuel savings by 30%, and lower the subsidy cost per marginal adoption by 29%.In a counterfactual without demand distortions, the abatement cost rises to US$137 per tCO 2 e. Contexts with large demand distortions could offer many cost-effective opportunities for climate change mitigation financing.
focus_rationale: The paper is a field experiment with charcoal users in Kenya on clean cooking subsidies, so it studies a single emerging/developing economy. Its link to markets is indirect, centred on climate-mitigation subsidy design and credit constraints.

title: The Robust Properties of Economies with Endogenous Production Networks
abstract: We characterize equilibria in a canonical class of economies with endogenous production networks, showing that log-prices equal a min-max over networks of a primitive affine function of logproductivities.This formula captures how resilience and fragility interact: the "min" reflects resilience from substituting suppliers, while the "max" reflects fragility from complementarityinduced rigidity.Applying these results, we generalize Hulten's theorem, finding that local Domar weights are generally insufficient to describe propagation of even small shocks.Moreover, we characterize how microeconomic volatility affects GDP, finding that smooth changes in Domar weights overstate its adverse effects by omitting option value from switching suppliers.
focus_rationale: The paper is a theoretical characterization of general equilibrium economies with endogenous production networks, with no particular country focus.

title: The Impact of Social Insurance on Household Debt
abstract: This paper investigates how the expansion of social insurance affects households' accumulation of debt.Insurance can reduce reliance on debt by lessening the financial impact of adverse events such as illness and job loss.But it can also weaken the motive to self-insure through savings, and households' improved financial resilience can increase access to credit.Using data on 10 million people and a quasi-experimental research design, we estimate the causal effect of expanded insurance on household debt, exploiting ZIP-level heterogeneity in exposure to the staggered expansions of one of the largest US social insurance programs: Medicaid.We find that a 1 percentage point increase in a ZIP code's Medicaid-eligible population increases credit card borrowing by 0.38%.Decomposing this effect in a model of household borrowing, we show that increased credit supply in response to households' improved financial resilience drives the rise in borrowing and contributes 30% of the net welfare gains of expanding Medicaid.
focus_rationale: The paper studies US Medicaid expansions and US household credit card borrowing, so it is about an advanced economy.

title: Pricing Power in the Mortgage Market: Evidence from GSE Fee Waivers
abstract: Market power may arise not only from firms, but also from individual salespeople who can exploit informational advantages over consumers.We explore this phenomenon in the mortgage market by examining a Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac fee waiver targeted at lower-income first-time homebuyers.We estimate that mortgage intermediaries capture over 60% of $1.5 billion in total fee waivers during 2023-2024, rather than fully passing these savings through to borrowers.Pass-through varies substantially across loan officers: those with a track record of originating expensive mortgages (independent of lender pricing) pass through less than 20% of the waiver.Our evidence suggests that loan officers retain incentives to steer borrowers into higher-rate mortgages, despite post-crisis regulations designed to limit such practices.
focus_rationale: The paper studies the US mortgage market and the Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac fee waiver for US first-time homebuyers, so it is mainly about an advanced economy.

title: Home-Foreign Elasticity Functions and the Gains from Trade
abstract: Gains from trade are typically calculated using a constant trade elasticity estimated from substitution across foreign countries.For general homothetic preferences, we show how to calculate these gains from the initial domestic expenditure share and the home-foreign elasticity function along a price path to autarky.While this function generally depends on the specific price path, under weak separability it does not.We provide conditions for its nonparametric identification and estimate sector-level elasticity functions using tariff changes implied by trade agreements.Across WIOD and OECD ICIO data, estimated home-foreign elasticities generally rise with domestic expenditure shares.Using estimated elasticity functions in a multi-sector model with intermediate inputs, the median gain across the WIOD countries is 19.37 log points, compared with 24.43 when each country-sector elasticity is held fixed at its initial value.
focus_rationale: The paper estimates sector-level trade elasticities across WIOD and OECD ICIO data covering many countries, so it is cross-country and methodological rather than focused on one economy group.

title: Credit Markets with New Screening Technologies
abstract: We study equilibrium market structure in a model of credit-market competition with correlated or uncorrelated screening errors and endogenous screening technologies.A pool externality arises because rejected borrowers reapply elsewhere, so lenders' screening and pricing choices affect competitors' applicant pools.With independent errors, a single market segment emerges, with rates rising smoothly as lenders who choose better technologies lend to more adversely selected borrowers.With correlated screening errors, potentially stemming from similar AI systems and overlapping financial-sector data, ex-ante identical lenders instead specialize across qualitatively distinct segments, generating a hockey-stick interest-rate schedule: segments with uniform rates but heterogeneous borrower quality coexist with segments featuring uniform quality but dispersed rates, echoing traditional banking, fintech, and high-rate indiscriminate lending.We show how technological and regulatory changes affecting screening costs, including frontier AI innovation and various forms of open banking, unevenly affect financial access and can either benefit or harm financially excluded borrowers.
focus_rationale: This is a theoretical model of credit-market competition with no specific economy studied, so it is Transversal.

title: Are We Consuming Too Much Groundwater?
abstract: We study the optimality of human groundwater extraction from many of the world's 3,400 aquifers, where institutional or market failures may produce non-optimal extraction decisions.We use remote sensing and economic data to estimate a dynamic model of water extraction for each aquifer, recover the discount factor that rationalizes observed groundwater extraction, and compare it against Ramsey and market benchmarks.Three-to four-fifths of aquifers are extracted more rapidly than is optimal, decreasing aquifer present value by several percent, and creating trillions of dollars in present value welfare losses.Policies that guarantee users constant water quantities indefinitely, through subsidies or prior appropriation, or policy rules that fully discount future extraction, generate larger welfare costs.A sustainable extraction path that maintains current fill forever generates meaningfully lower welfare than the optimal extraction path, because most aquifer stocks are already inefficiently low.
focus_rationale: The paper studies groundwater extraction across many of the world's aquifers, covering countries worldwide rather than a particular advanced or emerging group.

title: From Politics to Process: Evidence from Progressive Era Naturalizations
abstract: States that delegate governance to local officials face a trade-off between the benefits of local knowledge and the costs of biased administrators.Can imposing federal standards discipline bias and improve uniformity?We study this question by examining the introduction of federal standards to apply for citizenship under the 1906 Naturalization Act.Using newly-digitized census records covering over five million immigrants and a 30-year period, we show that standardizing adjudication of citizenship applications resulted in rapid convergence of naturalization practices across cities.While naturalizations were around 30% higher in election years pre-reform, this electoral cycle disappeared after the introduction of federal standards.Exploiting the staggered adoption of municipal civil service reforms aimed at removing patronage during the Progressive Era, we find that the reduction in political cycles was strongest in unreformed cities.Finally, the contraction in election year naturalizations changed the composition of new citizens.Affected cohorts earned 7% more, were more likely to enter citizenship-restricted occupations, and gave children more Americanized names.Our results thus show that standardizing administrative procedures can discipline politically-biased policy implementation.
focus_rationale: The paper studies US cities and federal naturalization rules during the Progressive Era, so it is about a single advanced economy, the United States. Its link to markets is weak, centring on public administration and immigrant labour outcomes.

title: A Model of U.S. Monetary Policy and the Global Financial Cycle
abstract: We propose a general equilibrium model in which U.S. monetary policy affects global risk premia by revaluing the wealth of currency-mismatched arbitrageurs.Assuming their portfolios are meanvariance efficient, arbitrageurs must be short the dollar.A U.S. tightening thus erodes arbitrageurs' net worth and raises the global price of risk.We discipline this mechanism to rationalize the effects of U.S. monetary policy on international asset prices, and we quantify the associated macroeconomic spillovers and role of policy responses abroad.In a potential future with higher dollar interest rates, arbitrageurs' dollar funding and U.S. monetary policy spillovers are dampened.
focus_rationale: The paper models how U.S. monetary policy drives the global financial cycle through global risk premia and dollar funding of arbitrageurs, with spillovers to international asset prices across countries rather than a particular economy or group. It is a global general equilibrium model, so it is Transversal.

title: Modeling and Evaluating the Labor Market and Fiscal Effects of Immigration
abstract: Immigration affects natives through both labor markets and public budgets, yet these channels are usually studied separately.We combine them in a general-equilibrium model with search-andmatching frictions, skill-specific progressive labor taxes, capital taxation and public goods, calibrated to 17 OECD countries over 2015-2019.The welfare effect on natives of a onepercentage-point increase in immigrant inflows varies in sign and size across countries, hinging on immigrants' skill mix, immigrant-native wage gaps, resident unemployment, and tax progressivity.For inflows matching the skill composition of 2019-2024 arrivals, native welfare rises in 14 of 17 economies, and in most cases both skill groups gain, through different channels.Lower-skilled natives gain mainly from higher pre-tax earnings, driven by job creation and complementarity with skilled immigrants; higher-skilled natives gain mainly from lower labor-tax burdens.Evaluating immigration policy thus requires modeling labor-market and fiscal channels jointly: either channel alone gives an incomplete picture of who gains and why.
focus_rationale: The model is calibrated to 17 OECD countries without a particular focus on advanced or emerging economies, so it covers both groups in a cross-country framework.

title: Foreign Giants' Broad Shoulders: The Causal Effect of Foreign Ideas on U.S. Innovation
abstract: We study the role of foreign ideas in U.S. innovation by constructing a directed "genealogy" of technologies from the full text of 13 million patents filed between 1887 and 2024.By tracing which earlier technologies appear in the founding patents of new ones, we recover a large-scale inputoutput network of technological recombination that identifies the foreign technologies that serve as inputs into innovation in the United States.We report four main findings.First, foreign ideas are pervasive: 54% of U.S. technologies build on at least one foreign input, and the most fertile U.S. technologies rely on foreign inputs most heavily.Second, foreign ideas have large causal effects on U.S. innovation.Using the historical settlement of migrants as a source of exogenous variation in local ancestry, we show that U.S. counties more exposed to knowledge from a given foreign country absorb substantially more technologies from that country and, in turn, invent significantly more U.S. technologies building on them.Third, foreign ideas shape not only the level but also the direction of technical change: U.S. counties are far more likely to pioneer the specific technologies whose foreign inputs are already in their local idea stock, and the changing origins of foreign ideas accompany the shift of American innovation from its historical heartland toward the coasts.Fourth, these effects leave a lasting imprint on local labor markets: decades later, counties that absorbed more of an origin's ideas host more jobs working with those ideas, and even more work with the U.S. technologies descended from them.
focus_rationale: The paper studies the causal effect of foreign technological ideas on U.S. innovation and local labour markets, so it centres on the United States, an advanced economy. Foreign origins are treated as sources of knowledge rather than as economies whose focus would shift the classification.

title: The Net Present Value of the California Billionaire Tax Act
abstract: This paper examines the revenue and migration impact of the 2026 California Billionaire Tax Act, a one-time 5 percent tax on the worldwide net worth of individuals exceeding $1 billion.Using data from the Forbes Billionaire List, news reports detailing the residential real estate holdings of California billionaires, and public announcements of billionaire departures from the state, we estimate the behavioral response and associated revenue loss to this new tax using several different methodologies.Even before accounting for reductions in other tax bases such as the income tax, we estimate that the Act will collect approximately $30 billion (range $28 to 36 billion), less than a third of the $100 billion projected by Galle et al. (2025).This range accounts for the publicly confirmed taxpayer migration that has already eliminated nearly 30 percent of the Act's wealth tax base, applies a litigation-survival discount to the remaining base, and is validated by the wealth tax base elasticity literature.We estimate that California's billionaires contribute $3.3-5.8 billion annually in state income taxes.The present value of permanently lost income tax collections from departures more than offsets the one-time wealth tax revenue, yielding a net present value of negative $38.9 billion.Across 100,000 simulated revenue and discount rate combinations, 85 percent of plausible outcomes produce a negative net present value of state revenues.
focus_rationale: The paper studies the fiscal and migration effects of a proposed wealth tax on billionaires in California, a US state within a developed economy.

title: Export Controls and the Economics of National Security
abstract: Export controls restrict trade to limit adversaries' access to goods that contribute to military capability, but their effectiveness depends on how trade and production adjust across countries.We combine new data on U.S. export control classifications and licensing outcomes with a quantitative general equilibrium model featuring dual-use production, input-output linkages, and separate civilian and military final expenditure.We estimate large export and entry frictions from these controls.These effects are substantially smaller for U.S. exports to members of multilateral export control regimes (MECRs): the differential is equivalent to an export cost of 15 to 29 log points.Relative to a counterfactual without differential controls on adversaries, multilateral controls reduce their imports of controlled products far more than unilateral U.S. controls.Only 7% of the reduction in controlled exports under the multilateral regime is replaced by other countries, compared with 28% under unilateral U.S. policy.Multilateral controls reduce adversaries' real military expenditure by increasing their military price index.The security impact, measured as U.S. real military expenditure relative to adversaries, rises by about 1 log point under multilateral controls but only 0.14 log points under unilateral controls, with both imposing a similar civilian real cost.Even a U.S. embargo fails to reproduce the multilateral security outcome.
focus_rationale: The paper studies US export controls and their effects on trade and military spending across adversary and allied countries, using a global general equilibrium model rather than focusing on a specific economy group. It has a weak link to markets through trade flows and production.

title: Conversations at Scale: Robust AI-led Interviews
abstract: The advent of large language models (LLMs) creates new opportunities to conduct qualitative interviews at scale, with thousands of respondents, thereby bridging qualitative and quantitative methods. We develop a simple, versatile approach for researchers to run AI-led qualitative interviews, including voice interviews. We assess its robustness by drawing comparisons to human experts and with several respondents-based quality metrics. The versatility of the approach is illustrated through four broad classes of applications: eliciting key factors in decision making, political views, subjective mental states, and mental models of the effects of public policies. High performance ratings are obtained in all of these domains. Our applications highlight the potential of AI-led interviews as a tool for measurement, hypothesis generation, and discovering mechanisms.
focus_rationale: The paper is a methodological contribution on AI-led qualitative interviews with no specific economy studied; applications cover decision making, political views and policy mental models in general terms.

title: Robust Aggregation of Correlated Information
abstract: Decisions are typically made by drawing on multiple sources of information, yet the correlation among these sources is often hard to assess. We study robustly optimal strategies—those that maximize the worst-case payoff guarantee across all correlation structures. With two states and two actions, the robustly optimal strategy is strikingly simple: use only the best information source and ignore the rest. With more actions, a robustly optimal strategy decomposes the problem into local comparisons and assigns each comparison to the source that is best at that comparison. With more states, the same specialization logic survives through a concavification characterization: the decision problem is decomposed into payoff-relevant components, and each component is assigned to its best source. These results offer a new rationale for why ignoring information can be optimal and highlight the benefit of using specialized information sources when correlations are ambiguous.
focus_rationale: The paper is a theoretical decision-theory study of robust aggregation of information sources under ambiguous correlation, with no specific economy studied.

title: When Should We (Not) Interpret Linear IV Estimands as LATE?
abstract: In this paper I revisit the interpretation of the linear instrumental variables (IV) estimand as a weighted average of conditional local average treatment effects (LATEs). I focus on a situation in which additional covariates are required for identification while the reduced-form and first-stage regressions may be misspecified due to an implicit homogeneity restriction on the effects of the instrument. I show that the weights on some conditional LATEs are negative and the IV estimand is no longer interpretable as a causal effect under a weaker version of monotonicity, i.e. when there are compliers but no defiers at some covariate values and defiers but no compliers elsewhere. The problem of negative weights disappears in the interacted specification of Angrist and Imbens (I1995), which avoids misspecification and seems to be underused in applied work. I illustrate my findings in an application to the causal effects of pretrial detention on case outcomes. In this setting, I reject the stronger version of monotonicity, demonstrate that the interacted instruments are sufficiently strong for consistent estimation using the jackknife methodology, and present several estimates that are economically and statistically different, depending on whether the interacted instruments are used.
focus_rationale: This is a methodological econometrics paper on interpreting linear IV estimands as weighted LATEs, with no particular economy as its focus. Its empirical application is to pretrial detention outcomes, which is applied legal and criminal-justice economics rather than market-relevant research.

title: A Model of Enclosures: Coordination, Conflict, and Efficiency in the Transformation of Land Property Rights
abstract: Economists and historians have long debated how open-access areas, frontier regions, and customary landholding regimes transformed into private property. This paper analyzes decentralized enclosure processes using the theory of aggregative games, examining how population density, enclosure costs, potential productivity gains, and local governance capacity, including the power to demand compensation, jointly determine the mix of property regimes. Depending on these fundamentals, private decisions to enclose may be strategic complements or substitutes. Strategic complements generate tipping points and socially destructive property races, whereas strategic substitutes produce smoother transitions and may leave enclosure below the social optimum. While policies to strengthen customary governance or compensate displaced stakeholders can realign incentives, addressing one distortion while neglecting others can worsen welfare.
focus_rationale: This is a theoretical model of enclosure dynamics using aggregative games, with no specific economy studied; it applies to historical and frontier land transformations in general.

title: Optimal Flood Insurance in a Second-Best World: Fiscal Spillovers, Reclassification Risk, and Moral Hazard
abstract: Intensifying climate change makes protection against natural disaster risk – either through ex ante insurance or ex post aid – a first-order public policy issue. Flood risk protection in the U.S. traditionally featured ex post aid through FEMA and heavily subsidized insurance through the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP). In an effort to correct subsidy-induced overbuilding and under-mitigation in flood-prone areas, the NFIP recently moved to actuarially fair insurance premiums. But this change has two unintended consequences: a fiscal spillover onto FEMA disaster aid as insurance coverage declines in flood-prone areas, and household exposure to uninsurable reclassification risk from uncertain climate projections. We develop a model of optimal flood insurance that incorporates the static and dynamic tradeoffs of subsidizing premiums. We then use a variety of identification strategies and data to estimate the five key parameters needed to implement this model. We find that the fiscal spillover and reclassification risk protection benefits significantly outweigh the moral hazard costs, and that the optimal subsidy to flood insurance is 51%, comparable to the level of subsidization before the recent reform.
focus_rationale: The paper studies the US National Flood Insurance Program and FEMA disaster aid, so it is about a single advanced economy.

title: How New Products Enter Markets: Social Networks, Consumer Imports, and Retailer Learning
abstract: This paper studies how new varieties enter markets and become locally available. We provide causal evidence of demand externalities that operate in two steps. First, information about new varieties diffuses directly through real-world social ties among consumers. Second, early purchases generate an indirect spillover to firms: local retailers learn from “pioneer” consumers which new varieties are most likely to succeed and adjust their product offerings accordingly. We study this process in the context of direct-to-consumer imports. Using customs records on individuals’ purchases matched to population-wide social networks, international migrant links, and retailer catchment areas, we document economically meaningful demand externalities. Product-specific expenditure shocks abroad transmit through migrant networks and shift which varieties consumers purchase. Leveraging these shocks as a plausibly exogenous source of local demand variation, we show strong peer effects: prior purchases by close neighbors, coworkers, or friends increase an individual’s likelihood of purchasing the same variety, especially for premium and visible goods. We leverage this result to identify an indirect spillover from consumers to firms: retailers are more likely to add a variety to their assortment when it becomes popular among consumers in their catchment area. Combining the instrument with linked consumer–retailer data and a self-conducted retailer survey, we show that this response reflects learning about latent demand for varieties not yet stocked locally. Together, social diffusion and retailer learning generate demand multipliers that reshape local product availability and expand access to global variety.
focus_rationale: The paper studies direct-to-consumer imports and social networks using customs records and migrant links, with the data and retailer catchment areas spanning a single setting that is not clearly one market group; the economies named are not specified in the abstract, so it is treated as cross-country and micro-focused.

title: Headwind or tailwind? How banks interpret borrowers’ AI exposure
abstract: General-purpose technologies create large opportunities but make their distribution across firms difficult to assess in real time. We use banks as interpreters of the rise of generative AI by studying lender-specific probability-of-default (PD) estimates for private firms in four large euro-area economies. As public attention to AI rises after ChatGPT, banks lower assessed default risk for borrowers in highly AI-exposed industries by about 5%. The reassessment is weaker for labor-intensive firms and stronger among lenders with pre-existing industry expertise. Yet the favorable industry-level effect is accompanied by a systematic reordering within product markets: banks reassess firms with stronger pre-ChatGPT market positions less favorably relative to their competitors, compressing the risk advantage associated with market leadership. Credit allocation moves in the same direction, with market leaders experiencing relatively lower drawn and committed credit, more relationship exits, and fewer new lenders. The reordering also predicts subsequent bad-credit events beyond banks’ consensus PDs. Internal bank assessments therefore provide a forward-looking measure of how generative AI is expected to reshape competitive risk.
focus_rationale: The paper studies bank-assessed default probabilities for private firms in four large euro-area economies, all advanced economies. Euro area members are classed as DM.

title: Competing rails for crossborder payments: banks, fintechs, and stablecoins
abstract: Cross-border payments remain slow and expensive despite significant improvements in digital financial infrastructure over the past several decades.
focus_rationale: The paper addresses cross-border payment systems globally, comparing banks, fintechs and stablecoins without a specific economy focus.

title: Inflation after the Iran war
abstract: An unexpected increase in energy costs raises inflation directly through flexibly-set prices. Whether that shock amplifies to a larger and persistent rise in inflation depends on its transmission through the economy.
focus_rationale: The abstract discusses a general energy-cost shock and its transmission to inflation without naming specific economies, so it applies across countries rather than to one group.

title: Central banks and macro financial stability in a fragmented global economy
abstract: The 25th BIS Annual Conference took place in Basel, Switzerland on 26 June 2026. The event brought together a distinguished group of central bank Governors, leading academics and former public officials to exchange views on the theme “Central banks and macro-financial stability in a fragmented global economy”.
focus_rationale: This is a conference announcement with no specific economies studied; its theme is global, covering central banks and financial stability in a fragmented world economy.

title: FEDS Note: Introducing Private Credit into the Financial Accounts of the United States
abstract: Katie Brinkman, Christine Dobridge , Tim Dore , Simon Glossner , Elizabeth Holmquist , Nam Nguyen, Maria Perozek , and Irina Stefanescu Over the past decade, private credit has played an increasingly important role in providing funding to middle-market businesses. While there are several definitions of private credit, here we define it as privately negotiated loans to businesses that are originated by nonbank investment funds rather than by traditional financial intermediaries such as banks.
focus_rationale: The paper introduces private credit into the US Financial Accounts, so it studies the United States economy specifically. It concerns nonbank lending to middle-market businesses.

title: FEDS Note: Ripples in the Reserve Pool: Unveiling Liquidity Signals from the Federal Funds Market
abstract: Sriya Anbil , Sebastian Infante, and Zeynep Senyuz When the Federal Reserve shifted to an ample-reserves framework, many observers started to question the relevance of the fed funds market. With reserves ample or abundant and rates anchored by administered floors, interbank borrowing declined sharply, and the market appeared to serve mainly as an arbitrage venue for non-bank institutions.
focus_rationale: The paper studies the US federal funds market and the Federal Reserve's ample-reserves framework, so it is about an advanced economy.

title: FEDS Note: Government Bonds’ Safe-Haven Property and Inflationary Pressures
abstract: Canlin Li and Emre Yoldas Earlier this year, escalation of the conflict in the Middle East resulted in sharp declines in major stock indexes as energy prices rose and the global economic outlook deteriorated, but prices of long-term government bonds in major advanced economies also declined (Figure 1). This prompted some commentators to question the premise that government bonds in these major advanced economies will rally in times of increased risk aversion and serve as a safe haven for investors (see for example, Kim, 2026).
focus_rationale: The note examines long-term government bonds in major advanced economies, which the abstract describes as the US and other advanced markets, responding to a Middle East conflict and energy price shock.

title: Offshore forwards and exchange rate transmission in emerging markets
abstract: We study how offshore non-deliverable forward (NDF) markets transmit exchange-rate pressures to domestic currency markets. Using unique transaction-level data on the universe of centrally cleared NDFs for ten emerging-market currencies over 2013–2025, we show that offshore NDF order flow moves both offshore forward and domestic spot exchange rates and widens the offshore–onshore forward spread.
focus_rationale: The paper studies ten emerging-market currencies using offshore NDF and onshore spot data, so it is about EM exchange rate dynamics.

title: Revenue per Worker Is Up. Are Firms Getting a Larger Share?
abstract: From the Great Recession until 2019, U.S. labor productivity growth disappointed. Nonfarm-business output per hour grew about 1 percent a year from 2010 to 2019, down from 3 percent in the late 1990s. This slowdown was especially pronounced in manufacturing, and it coincided with a slowdown in the growth of revenue per worker among public firms. However, since 2019, growth has picked up to twice the 2010s rate, around 2 percent. In this post, I use data from firms’ 10-K filings to unpack this recent acceleration. I first show that the acceleration appears in public firms’ revenue per worker, then document how the gains went into profit margins, and finally, what firm characteristics predicted significant profit margin increases. The increase in profit margins is consistent with ongoing declines in the labor share of output.
source_name: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
focus_rationale: The paper studies US public firms' revenue per worker, profit margins and productivity using 10-K filings, so it is about a single advanced economy.

title: When less is more: behavioral effects of CBDC holding limits
abstract: Holding limits are a central design feature of proposed retail central bank digital currencies (CBDC). While such limits mechanically prevent individuals from exceeding a maximum balance, they may also generate behavioral responses whose directions are a priori unclear. We conducted an incentivized online experiment with participants from four euro-area countries, exogenously varying the presence and level of a holding limit to causally separate direct mechanical effects from behavioral effects. We find that behavioral responses increase holdings of the means of payment subject to the holding limit, consistent with an attraction effect. This effect is material only when the limit is high enough. Enabling reverse waterfall —automatic conversion into this limited means of payment— increases adoption while reducing holdings. These results suggest that combining holding limits with automatic funding mechanisms can support CBDC use while containing holdings, thereby helping to mitigate potential financial stability risks.
focus_rationale: The experiment recruits participants from four euro-area countries, all advanced economies, so the paper is about DM retail CBDC design in the euro area.

title: Stop believing in haircuts - at least the way you think about them
abstract: We study how frictions impact haircut setting in repo markets. Using transaction-level supervisory data and exploiting the 2021 introduction of the binding leverage ratio requirement, we show that three frictions jointly shape haircuts in the bilateral dealer-to-client segment: dealer balance sheet constraints, collateral convenience yields, and client outside options. In collateral-driven repos, binding leverage constraints and broader client outside options both raise haircuts, while higher convenience yields push them down. In funding-driven trades, the leverage constraint has no effect, higher convenience yields raise haircuts through the rehypothecation channel, and broader client outside options lower them. We rationalise these patterns in a bilateral bargaining model with periodic haircut renegotiation. Consistent with the model, constrained dealers exhibit higher repo-rate volatility and weaker pass-through of ECB policy rate changes in the collateral-driven segment. Post-crisis bank regulation thus carries potential unintended consequences for repo market functioning and the transmission of monetary policy.
focus_rationale: The abstract uses transaction-level supervisory data on the bilateral dealer-to-client repo segment and does not name specific economies. Its focus is euro-area-style repo markets and ECB policy pass-through, but the paper's economies are not explicitly stated, so it is classed as Transversal.

title: Chokepoint disruptions and their macroeconomic consequences
abstract: Rising geopolitical tensions, including trade restrictions and conflicts, are increasingly disrupting global supply chains, posing significant risks at critical chokepoints. Strong substitution effects and the use of inventories have helped to mitigate adverse output effects of chokepoint disruptions, but they often come at the cost of higher input prices. An effective policy response to chokepoint disruptions requires a tailored approach that takes account of the cause, centrality and the private sector’s ability to substitute and draw on buffers.
focus_rationale: The paper studies supply-chain chokepoint disruptions in general terms, with no particular economy as its focus, so it is cross-country and global in scope.

title: Has the AI Boom Impacted the U.S. Current Account?
abstract: The AI boom is showing up in different corners of the U.S. economy, including international trade. Imports of semiconductors, servers, and computing equipment have climbed sharply yet the U.S. current account deficit has been largely unchanged. To better understand how the AI boom has not substantially affected the trade balance, consider that the current account is dictated by the gap between domestic saving and investment spending. It turns out that aggregate saving and investment spending have not changed much during the AI boom. Aggregate investment has not risen due to weakness outside the AI sector and business saving has remained robust.
source_name: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
focus_rationale: The paper studies the United States, an advanced economy, examining how the AI investment boom has affected the US current account and trade balance.

title: FEDS Note: The Rise of Semiliquid Funds for Retail Investors
abstract: Logan George and Chaehee Shin Investment funds differ in how investors can access their capital. The redemption rules governing how and when investors can withdraw have evolved endogenously in response to shifting investor demand and regulatory constraints. While the immediate liquidity of open-end mutual funds and exchange-traded funds has long dominated the retail market, the landscape has been evolving over time.
focus_rationale: The note examines the US fund industry and retail investor access to semiliquid funds, which is a US-focused study of fund structures. It is indirectly relevant to markets via fund liquidity and redemption dynamics.

title: FEDS Paper: A Macroeconomic Analysis of Household Labor Supply Responses to Large Fiscal Transfers
abstract: Isabel Cairó , Shigeru Fujita, and Camilo Morales-Jimenez The fiscal transfers deployed during the COVID-19 pandemic were unprecedented in scale and strongly progressive. Using CPS/ASEC data, we document that the decline in employment during the pandemic was larger for low-income households and tightly linked to the intensity of transfer receipt, a pattern absent during the Global Financial Crisis. We develop and estimate a two-sector, heterogeneous-household general equilibrium model in which low-income households are borrowing-constrained in normal times but can save out of sufficiently large transfers. Because preferences permit wealth effects on labor supply, transfers both reduce labor supply and raise consumption, and a dollar of transfers is split roughly evenly between the two margins. We find that the effects of transfers are state-dependent: because the borrowing constraint binds more tightly in a deeper recession, the same transfer relaxes a tighter constraint and delivers an employment and consumption response about 40 to 50 percent larger during the pandemic than when the same transfer is introduced in the steady state. In the model, transfers were welfare-improving for recipients, with gains diminishing as transfers increase.
focus_rationale: The paper studies US household labor supply and fiscal transfers during the COVID-19 pandemic, using CPS/ASEC data and a model calibrated to the US economy.

title: What analysts hear and why it matters for monetary policy
abstract: We introduce a novel measure of how European Central Bank (ECB) monetary policy is interpreted by analysts at major investment banks. We construct a “policy interpretation shock” based on the language used in analysts’ reports covering monetary policy decisions by the ECB’s Governing Council (GovC). The main identifying assumption is that changes in the way analysts report on policy communication by the GovC—that is, the change in the policy tone from the preview report to the recap report—reflect unexpected information revealed by the policy event. Using GPT-based sentiment extraction, we show that the tone in these reports closely tracks that of the GovC, often even anticipating shifts in tone. Changes in the policy tone before and after meetings capture how market intermediaries interpret and adjust their assessment of policy decisions. These interpretation shocks are followed by contractionary macroeconomic responses and systematic movements in financial-market prices. These findings underscore the important role of communication in shaping expectations and influencing economic outcomes.
focus_rationale: The paper studies how analysts interpret ECB monetary policy decisions and the resulting macro and financial-market responses, all in the euro area, which is an advanced economy bloc.

title: The heterogeneous bank lending channel of monetary policy
abstract: How does heterogeneity in banks’ interest-rate risk exposure shape monetary policy transmission? We develop a quantitative macroeconomic model of heterogeneous banks to answer this question. We establish an irrelevance result: differences in interest-rate risk exposure between fixed- and variable-rate banking systems matter for transmission only when bank solvency concerns become relevant. Calibrating the model to the euro area, we show that idiosyncratic default risk pushes a substantial share of banks toward the solvency threshold, making heterogeneity quantitatively important. When policy rates rise, fixed-rate banks suffer net interest margin compression—funding costs increase while legacy loan income stays unchanged—eroding capital and triggering sharper deleveraging. The lending elasticity to monetary policy is one-third larger in fixed-rate economies. The effects extend to financial stability: tightening raises bank failure rates in fixed-rate systems while lowering them in variable-rate systems. The results provide a rationale for macroprudential and monetary policy coordination and for monetary policy gradualism.
focus_rationale: The paper calibrates a quantitative model to the euro area, a advanced economy, and studies how monetary policy transmits through bank interest-rate risk exposure there.

title: Money and the architecture of trust
abstract: Money is one of the most consequential social institutions humanity has built. Starting from the most elementary monetary act, a payment, this paper provides an account of how money works, grounded in the tradition of credit theories of money.
focus_rationale: The paper is a conceptual account of how money works, grounded in credit theories of money, with no particular country or economy as its focus.

title: How is Labor Demand Changing as AI Improves? New Global Evidence
abstract: The rapid advance of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has sparked intense debate about its effects on labor markets. We draw on over 700 million online job postings to present new evidence covering 110 economies. Demand has declined by nearly 10 percent in more AI-exposed occupations but, surprisingly, this impact has stabilized even as AI has become more capable. To understand this pattern, we develop a novel measure of AI adoption based on references to emerging AI skills in job postings. Demand for these skills has grown rapidly, particularly in more exposed occupations. Indeed, firms with stronger demand for AI skills exhibit faster growth in job postings, even in more exposed occupations. AI appears to be reshaping labor demand by both compressing hiring in more exposed occupations and generating new opportunities for workers with AI skills.
focus_rationale: The paper uses job postings from 110 economies spanning advanced and emerging markets, so it is cross-country rather than focused on either group.

title: Inverted Gravity
abstract: We invert structural gravity to recover trade cost changes delivering targeted outcomes.For attainable welfare targets, one instrument per target yields a unique solution.At unchanged producer prices and to first order, each instrument must change by the welfare target divided by its own expenditure share; the required domestic change is about the size of the target, while the import change is several times larger.Inverting observed trade flows gives a separate trade cost change for each of the two directions in which a pair of countries trades.Applications to NAFTA and world trade illustrate the benefits of our approach.
focus_rationale: The paper develops an inversion method for structural gravity models of trade costs and welfare, applied to NAFTA and world trade, so it is methodological and cross-country rather than focused on one market group.

title: When Cash Flows Turn Negative: Liquidity-Driven Selling by Pension Funds
abstract: Pension funds are long-horizon investors with predictable liability structures.As such, they are often perceived as investors who can provide liquidity and stabilize markets.However, pension funds increasingly face negative operating cash flows as benefit payments exceed contributions.Using aggregate data on U.S. public pension funds combined with granular holdings obtained through public records requests, we document three findings that challenge the conventional view of pension funds as stabilizing investors.First, pension funds with more negative cash flows do not adjust their target asset allocations and maintain low allocations to safe and liquid assets.Second, because of these limited safe asset buffers, pension funds meet cash flow shocks primarily by selling equities, absorbing $0.67 per dollar of shock through equity sales.At the security level, pension funds sell across equities rather than following a safe and liquid-assets-first approach.Third, pension funds sell equities even when equity returns are negative, indicating that these trades reflect liquidity needs rather than portfolio rebalancing.Together, these findings show that pension funds have become regular sellers in equity markets rather than contrarian, stabilizing investors.
focus_rationale: The paper studies U.S. public pension funds and their equity selling behaviour, so the economy studied is the United States, an advanced economy.

title: Do Judges Move Markets? Ideological Shifts in the Supreme Court and Macroeconomic Expectations
abstract: This paper studies how judicial ideology shapes financial markets' expectations about the macroeconomy.We use unexpected deaths of U.S. Supreme Court Justices as quasi-experimental shifts in the Court's ideological balance.High-frequency asset price responses reveal how markets perceive the macroeconomic consequences of these ideological shifts.We find that a more conservative Court is associated with lower inflation expectations, lower real activity expectations, and lower bond yields.A shift towards a more liberal Court induces the opposite responses.The finding that inflation and activity expectations respond with the same sign suggests that markets revise their expectations about aggregate demand, rather than aggregate supply.Moreover, contrasting the yield responses with estimates from studies of fiscal policy news indicates that a more conservative (liberal) Court leads markets to expect tighter (looser) future fiscal policy.We validate our quasi-experimental setup with sectoral asset price dynamics, such as high-frequency responses of clean energy and health care stocks.Taken together, our findings are consistent with markets interpreting changes in the Supreme Court's ideological composition as news about future fiscal expansions or contractions.
focus_rationale: The paper studies US Supreme Court ideological shifts and their effects on US market expectations for inflation, activity, bond yields and sectoral stocks. The economy studied is the United States, an advanced economy.

title: Estimating the Impact of Targeted Public Policies with Limited Data
abstract: Many public policies aim to support (or change the behavior of) a specific, targeted sub-group of the population.To measure the causal impacts of such policies, social scientists use quasi-experimental methods of policy evaluation, but are often hampered by data availability issues, especially regarding targeted populations, who are often disadvantaged and/or vulnerable.We use power calculations to quantify the challenge of detecting a policy's impact on a small minority population based on population level data, using the impact of abortion bans on economic welfare as an example.We provide insight into this challenge and a roadmap for how researchers can calculate, ex-ante, whether their study is sufficiently powered to detect reasonably meaningful effect sizes.
focus_rationale: The paper is a methodological study on power calculations for policy evaluation, using US abortion bans as an illustrative example rather than focusing on a particular economy's markets.

title: Affirmative Action in Centralized College Admissions Systems
abstract: We study the consequences of affirmative action in college admissions.We develop an empirical framework that distinguishes the effects on marginally benefited and displaced students from the overall effects of the policy.The overall effects include equilibrium reallocations as benefited students leave seats that others fill and displaced students take seats elsewhere, displacing others in turn.We apply this framework to a large-scale policy in Brazil that required all federal institutions to reserve half their seats for racially and socioeconomically disadvantaged applicants.Exploiting admissions cutoffs, we find that marginally benefited targeted students attend and graduate from higher-quality programs.Their graduation gains are about twice the losses of marginally displaced non-targeted students, reflecting targeted students' weaker outside options.To evaluate the overall effects, we estimate a model of degree choices and potential outcomes.Among all reallocated students, benefited students still gain nearly twice what displaced students lose, but equilibrium reallocations make the policy displace about 30%more students than it benefits.Non-targeted students' losses therefore offset about two-thirds of targeted students' graduation gains, leaving a modest net gain across all students.
focus_rationale: The paper studies Brazil's federal college admissions quota policy, a single emerging economy. Its link to markets is weak, covering education outcomes and labour-relevant graduation gains rather than pricing or policy transmission.

title: Strategic Complementarity and Persistence in Linear-Quadratic Mean Field Games
abstract: We study the relation between strategic complementarities and aggregate persistence in linearquadratic mean field games with interactions in states and actions.The framework provides local approximations to common macroeconomic problems, including capital accumulation and multiproduct pricing.We show that the equilibrium aggregate dynamics coincide with those of a single-agent linear-quadratic control problem in which state and action curvatures are adjusted for strategic interactions.This result gives conditions for equilibrium existence, establishes uniqueness, and links strategic interactions to aggregate adjustment.We establish conditions under which stronger state complementarities increase persistence, while stronger action complementarities reduce it, even in multidimensional problems whose underlying matrices are not simultaneously diagonalizable.Under these conditions, internalizing state complementarities makes the utilitarian planner's allocation more persistent, while internalizing action complementarities makes it less persistent.With common shocks, we give conditions under which individual and aggregate dynamics can be combined to identify strategic interactions and model parameters.Finally, we extend the analysis to interactions through higher moments of the state distribution.
focus_rationale: The paper is a theoretical and methodological study of linear-quadratic mean field games with no particular economy as its object; it illustrates with generic macro problems such as capital accumulation and pricing.

title: Measurement Error in Self-Reported Data on Stigmatized Behavior: Experimental Evidence on Intimate Partner Violence
abstract: Error in the measurement of key development outcomes affects our understanding of socioeconomic phenomena and their policy implications.This paper focuses on measuring intimate partner violence (IPV), a public health issue affecting women globally.We introduce a novel, privacy-enhancing data collection method using a ballot, comparing it to standard survey techniques in which responses are not kept private from enumerators, and list experiments, an approach ensuring complete anonymity.Our findings show that improved privacy yields higher and more accurate IPV reports than both, especially among women with low education.By linking our data with two natural experiments, we demonstrate that the non-random nature of underreporting with standard methods can lead to biased estimates of IPV determinants.
focus_rationale: The paper studies intimate partner violence measurement with survey data from developing-country settings, with no macro or financial angle. Its economies are not specified in the abstract, so the EM classification reflects the development context of the outcome.

title: Gains from Trade in Gun Policy: A Compensation-Based Benchmark
abstract: Policies restricting gun sales face substantial political opposition and constitutional constraints.In this paper, we ask how costly it would be to induce potential hand-gun buyers to choose less lethal alternatives.Pairing stated-choice experiments with a behavioral model of firearm choice, we estimate the payments required to induce substitution away from handguns toward long guns or no gun purchase.We then compare these payments with the resulting mortality benefits.We find substantial gains from trade: many prospective handgun buyers require relatively little compensation to switch and targeted compensation can avert homicides at a social cost well below conventional estimates of the value of a statistical life.The extent to which these gains can be realized through compensation, however, depends on the state's information about which consumers would change their choices and at what price.Without this information, uniform subsidies pay consumers who would choose an alternative anyway and overcompensate those willing to switch for less, sharply increasing government expenditure and reducing the optimal scale of compensation.
focus_rationale: The paper studies US handgun purchasing and firearm policy, a US-only setting. It is applied microeconomics with no direct market or macro link.

title: Industrial Policy via the IPO Market
abstract: This paper studies how China uses access to public equity markets as an instrument of industrial policy.We find that policy-favored status, rather than industry Tobin's Q, predicts IPO activity, in contrast to the United States.The effect is economically large: our estimates imply that favored industries had 287% more IPOs and 148% higher IPO proceeds than non-favored industries over 2002 to 2022.We develop a framework to interpret these findings: the government shapes the number of listing opportunities available across industries, while market forces determine which firms obtain these opportunities based on firm fundamentals.Consistent with our framework, policy favor also predicts a valuation premium which persists after listing.
focus_rationale: The paper studies China's use of IPO market access as industrial policy, comparing it with the United States. The focus is China, an emerging economy.

title: Access to Capital and the IPO Decision: An Analysis of US Private Firms
abstract: We analyze firms' IPO decisions using detailed financial data on US private firms.Firms with higher external capital needs are more likely to go public.Following the IPO, firms increase investment and debt issuance, leaving their leverage ratios un-changed from pre-IPO levels.Finally, newly public firms borrow from an expanded pool of lenders on improved terms, and the within-firm dispersion in banks' private risk assessments declines.Our analysis suggests that firms go public to improve their access to capital, which is facilitated by reduced asymmetric information, and that the benefit extends beyond the IPO itself to new sources of debt.
focus_rationale: The paper studies IPO decisions and financing of US private firms, so it is about an advanced economy. Its link to markets is indirect, through corporate access to equity and debt capital.

title: Road Pricing under Heterogeneity
